analysis.one_liner: Taxes investment gains over $1 million like wages and closes the inherited-gains tax break.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 17, 2026, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, money made from selling stocks or other investments is taxed at lower rates than paychecks, and if you hold an asset until death, the gain escapes income tax entirely for the heirs. This bill would tax gains above $1 million at the same rates as wages, treat assets passed by gift or at death as if they had been sold, cap some real estate and small-business tax breaks used by wealthy owners, and give heirs up to five years to pay the resulting tax. It includes a large carve-out for family farms and family businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary wage earners, whose income is taxed at full rates while large investment gains currently get a discount; the bill raises revenue from households with over $1 million in annual gains and from heirs to large estates. Family farms and family businesses get a 50% exclusion on gain above $1 million and the right to pay in installments.

how_it_helps.text: Limits the lower capital-gains and dividend tax rates to taxpayers whose total income stays at or below $1 million, so gains above that line are taxed at ordinary income rates [S2].
Treats property transferred by gift or at death as sold at its fair market value, ending the 'stepped-up basis' rule under which heirs' inherited gains currently escape income tax entirely [S2].

Excludes up to $1 million of gain per estate transfer from tax (adjusted for inflation), plus 50% of any gain above that from a qualifying family farm or family business, and lets heirs pay the tax on death-transfers in up to five annual installments at a reduced interest rate [S2].

Caps the deferral of gain through like-kind real estate exchanges at $500,000 per year and $1 million lifetime (farms exempted), and limits the 20% pass-through business income deduction to taxpayers with taxable income at or below $1 million [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Households with more than $1 million in annual capital gains or dividends, heirs to estates with over $1 million in unrealized gains (other than protected farms and businesses), large real estate investors who use like-kind exchanges, and owners of pass-through businesses earning over $1 million.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy investors, heirs, real estate traders

drawbacks.text: Heirs could owe tax on gains their parents never received in cash, forcing sales of illiquid assets like businesses or art to raise the money; the bill softens this with a $1 million exclusion and five-year installment payments, but does not eliminate it [S2].
Valuing unique assets at death is harder than reading a stock price, and the bill requires new reporting of gifts and death transfers, adding compliance work for executors and gift-givers [S2].

The family farm and business carve-out is complex: it requires a 10-year use certification, exempts 'hardship' sales from recapture, and lets buyers assume the recapture liability, giving well-advised owners room to plan around it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — ending the gap between how wages and large investment gains are taxed, and ending the step-up that lets heirs sell inherited assets tax-free — addresses a well-documented inequity that costs revenue. The design anticipates the hardest objections: it exempts the first $1 million of gain, shelters farms and family businesses, and spreads payments over five years at a reduced interest rate. The main honest concerns are valuation and liquidity problems for unusual assets and the complexity of the farm carve-out, which is real but secondary to the bill's central purpose.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the bill on March 17, 2026, joined by Sens. Sanders, Merkley, and Booker [S2].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that is the last recorded action [S4].
Three senators are cosponsoring: two Democrats and one Independent [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has lost anything — but if the bill dies in committee, wealthy households and heirs keep the current tax treatment, including the step-up in basis that lets inherited gains go untaxed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households, if it goes nowhere

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Equal Tax Act and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.name: Sens. Bernie Sanders, Jeff Merkley, and Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors (Sanders an Independent who caucuses with Democrats).

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 17, 2026; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled since.

against.name: Republican Senate majority
against.role: Controls the Senate calendar and the Finance Committee's agenda
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled any action on the bill, which would raise taxes on high-income households.

sides.party_line_note: All four original sponsors are Democrats or left-leaning Independents, and no Republican has signed on; Republicans hold the Senate majority and the Finance chairmanship in the 119th Congress.

industries.note: Investment gains above $1 million would be taxed at ordinary wage rates, and gains now passed to heirs untaxed would be taxed as deemed sales. Heirs and high-income investors bear the direct cost, offset by the $1 million exclusion, farm/business carve-outs, and installment payment rights.
Like-kind exchange deferral would be capped at $500,000 a year and $1 million lifetime, pushing large property swappers to pay tax they currently defer indefinitely.
The 20% qualified business income deduction would phase out above $1 million of taxable income, raising effective rates on high-earning partnership and S-corporation owners.

Death transfers of qualifying farm or business real property get a 50% exclusion on gain above $1 million, plus a special 10-year use certification and recapture regime — a lighter burden than other appreciated assets, but not full exemption.
The step-up rules they currently plan around would shrink, but new gift and death-transfer reporting and trust rules would generate compliance work.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress ends January 3, 2027. With Republicans controlling the Senate and the Finance Committee, and no scheduled action months after referral, the bill is very likely to die in committee without a vote, as comparable proposals to tax gains at death have in recent Congresses.
